name: Eettisseri Mana (Narikkode, Kunnamangalath)
tagline: Historic Namboothiri illam near Narikkode with ritual, theyyam and nagasthanam links
summary: A traditional Namboothiri ancestral house in Narikkode (Kunnamangalath), Kannur — noted locally for its age, temple shrines, theyyam connections and continued family stewardship.
description: Eettisseri Mana is a traditional Namboothiri illam in the Narikkode / Kunnamangalath area of Kannur district. Local reporting describes the house as several centuries old (commonly quoted as about 500 years) and still owned and managed by family representatives and a trust.

The mana sits in a compound that includes a pond and small family shrines; local sources record an associated nagasthanam (snake‑shrine) and a dedicated theyyam worship room where village ritual forms are kept and honoured. The property has attracted interest as a cultural location and for occasional film shoots.

For visitors the place is important as a living example of North Malabar Namboothiri ritual life — it illustrates links between ancestral homes, kavus (sacred groves/shrines), theyyam festivities and the temple/ritual calendar of the region.

Local tradition also links the wider Kannur Namboothiri world with practices such as manthravaadam (traditional mantric/thaṇthric remedies) and hereditary ritual roles; direct documentary evidence of mantravaadam specifically performed at Eettisseri Mana is limited in public sources, so those links are best described as local/traditional associations.

sections.heading: Background
body: Eettisseri Mana appears in local reporting as one of the historic Namboothiri ancestral houses near Narikkode (Kunnamangalath) in Kannur district; regional coverage describes the house as centuries old and still in family care.

The illam sits in the North Malabar ritual landscape where ancestral homes, kavus and village shrines are interwoven with theyyam practice and hereditary temple roles. Government/heritage listings for the area record a Narikkode Eettisseri nagasthanam associated with the family and name a family representative in local records.

sections.heading: What to see and do
body: Walk the outer compound (observe from public approaches unless you have permission). Visible features reported in local accounts include the traditional compound pond, multiple courtyards/rooms typical of an illam, and a room used historically for theyyam worship with images/objects of local ritual deities.

Look for the nagasthanam (family snake shrine) recorded in local land/forest listings — these groves and shrines are culturally important in North Malabar ritual practice. Note: many inner rooms, family shrines and ritual objects are private and access is controlled by the family/trust.

sections.heading: Plan your visit
body: Eettisseri Mana is not run as a public museum. Visitors should request permission from the family or trust before entering the property; confirm visiting arrangements locally and respect any restrictions around inner shrines or ritual timings.

Combine a visit with local cultural experiences in Kannur — theyyam performances (season roughly late October–May) and nearby kavus make the area richer for those interested in ritual traditions. Confirm dates and permissions before travel, and follow local guidance on photography and conduct.

visitorInfo.bestTime: October–March (dry season and main theyyam season; theyyam runs roughly late October–May).
visitorInfo.howToReach: By road from Kannur district towns. Use Taliparamba or Kannur as local reference points and ask locally for directions to Narikkode / Kunnamangalath; confirm access with the family/trust before visiting.
etiquette: Get permission from the family or managing trust before entering — the mana is privately stewarded.
Respect ritual spaces: ask before photographing shrines or ceremonies and follow local cues during theyyam or puja events.
Combine the visit with a theyyam calendar enquiry (Oct–May) if you want to witness live ritual performances.
Confirm exact location and opening/access arrangements locally; do not assume public access or fixed visiting hours.
